In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of intracellular calcium (Ca2+) stores in resting and activated T lymphocytes from the spleen of the rat.
intracellular calcium homeostasis of T lymphocytes.
the study of intracellular calcium stores of T lymphocyte, and the effects of activation on these stores.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the increase in total Ca2+ stores in the T lymphocyte is due to an enlargement of the ER, which is not necessarily accompanied by a parallel increase in the IP3‐sensitive pool.
the increase of intracellular calcium is not a consequence of the increase of the pool released by thapsigargin but is rather the result of an increase of the total pool of calcium.

the increase of the Ca2+ content in activated lymphocytes is due to an enlargement of the ER Ca2+ pool (which is insensitive to IP3 and, therefore, not involved in the Ca2+ signaling pathway) and of non‐ER pools.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Ca2+ stores are increased in activated lymphocytes and that this increase is due to an expansion of ER Ca2+ stores, in addition to an increase of the pool released by IP3.
the Ca2+ stores in resting and activated lymphocytes differ in size, composition, and functional properties.
the activation of T lymphocytes is associated with the appearance of a novel pool of Ca2+ which, in the resting cells, is not accessible to the Ca2+‐mobilizing agonists.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the intracellular Ca2 + stores are altered by T cell activation and that the alterations are different for in vitro and in vitro activation.
the intracellular Ca2+-stores of T lymphocytes are not static but rather dynamic structures that undergo significant changes during the course of activation.
intracellular calcium stores are altered by activation of T lymphocytes and this alteration is accompanied by changes in the expression of ER proteins.
